title: Carthage and Hannibal: The Enemy Rome Almost Lost To

cards.h: The city that nearly ruled the Mediterranean
cards.b:
For a long time Rome was one city-state among many. Its real test came from Carthage, a sea power in North Africa with ports across the western Mediterranean.

Between 264 and 146 BCE the two states fought three wars. The second one nearly ended with Hannibal marching into Italy. What would Europe look like if he had won?

Phoenician settlers from Tyre founded Carthage, in today's Tunisia. Later Roman writers dated it to 814 BCE, though the date is a tradition, not proof.

Carthage grew rich on trade in metal, purple dye and grain. It held Sicily, Sardinia and much of Spain. Its navy was feared and its merchants sailed far beyond the Strait of Gibraltar.

cards.h: The First Punic War over Sicily
cards.b:
The name Punic comes from the Latin word for Phoenician. The first war (264–241 BCE) was fought over Sicily. Rome built a fleet from scratch and beat Carthage at sea.

Carthage lost Sicily and had to pay a huge sum. Its general Hamilcar Barca then turned to Spain, and he raised a new army there for his family.

Polybius (c. 200–118 BCE)

A Greek who was held as a hostage in Rome, Polybius wrote the Histories, the best surviving account of the wars. He says that Hannibal, as a child, swore an oath at his father's altar to be an enemy of Rome.

Polybius is not neutral. He wanted to explain why Rome had become master of the Mediterranean, so read him with care.

cards.h: Five dates that shaped the war
cards.b: Hannibal led his army from Spain, over the Alps, into northern Italy in 218 BCE, with a few dozen war elephants. Most of them did not survive the cold.

cards.h: Cannae, the battle taught in military schools
cards.b:
In 216 BCE, at Cannae in southern Italy, Hannibal set up a curved line that gave way in the centre and then closed round the Roman army. The Romans lost tens of thousands of men in a single day.

Many later generals studied Cannae as a model of encirclement. Hannibal still could not take Rome itself. Its allies stayed loyal, and Rome refused to make peace.

cards.h: Scipio takes the fight to Africa
cards.b:
Rome's general Scipio decided to attack Carthage directly. He landed in North Africa and forced Hannibal home from Italy. At Zama in 202 BCE Scipio defeated him, and the Second Punic War ended.

Scipio took the name Africanus. Carthage gave up its navy and most of its empire, and it had to pay Rome a large indemnity over 50 years.

cards.h: Did Rome sow salt on Carthage?
cards.b:
A popular story says the Romans sowed the fields of Carthage with salt so nothing would grow again. It is a dramatic image, and many people repeat it.

Most historians doubt it. The sources are late and vague, and Roman writers did not agree on it. Rome did destroy Carthage in 146 BCE, but the salt story is probably a later legend. Historians argue how far the destruction went.

Scholars still debate the route of Hannibal's army over the Alps. Possible passes include the Little St Bernard, the Col de la Seigne and the Col du Clapier.

Each theory has supporters. Some use landscape and timing, others use the words of ancient writers. The debate shows how hard it is to rebuild a march that happened more than two thousand years ago.

cards.h: The last war and the end of Carthage
cards.b:
Hannibal went into exile and died in the 180s BCE at the court of King Prusias of Bithynia, in Asia Minor. Carthage slowly rebuilt its trade and its wealth.

Rome grew nervous about its rival. In 149 BCE it began the Third Punic War. After a siege of about three years, Carthage fell in 146 BCE, and Rome turned the land into a province called Africa.

When Zama was fought in 202 BCE, the Mauryan empire in India was breaking up. Ashoka had died about 232 BCE. In 185 BCE the Shunga dynasty took power in Magadha.

Within about twenty years, Greek kings from Bactria would rule parts of north-west India, and their coins carried both Greek and Indian scripts. The Mediterranean and Indian worlds were already touching.

Five things to remember
  1. Three Punic Wars were fought between Rome and Carthage from 264 to 146 BCE.
  2. Hannibal crossed the Alps in 218 BCE and won at Cannae in 216 BCE.
  3. Scipio beat Hannibal at Zama in 202 BCE.
  4. Carthage was destroyed in 146 BCE.
  5. Polybius is our key source, and he was biased toward Rome.
Think about it
  • Why did Rome keep going after a defeat that would have ended most states?
  • How much of the 'salt on the fields' story is memory and how much is propaganda?
